newsitem.title: UK: Stocks, bonds, dollar up in early election celebration.
newsitem.headline: Stocks, bonds, dollar up in early election celebration.

text.p: Stocks, bonds and the dollar all rose Tuesday as investors held a little party ahead of election results they were betting would be good for financial markets.
Oil edged lower and gold ended little changed.

The Dow Jones industrial average jumped 39.50 points to 6,081.18 as investors bet President Clinton would be re-elected and Republicans would keep control of the House, pointing to more modest economic growth and low inflation ahead.

The Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks rose 7.41 points to a record 714.14, beating the old milestone of 710.82 set on Oct. 18. The NYSE Composite index of all listed common stocks also set a record, rising 3.36 to 378.43.

The blue-chip Dow index drew close to its record of 6,094.23 set on Oct. 18. In the broader market, advancing issues led declines 1,447 to 945 on active volume of 486 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
"The market has predicted the election," said Larry Wachtel, an analyst at Prudential Securities.

"It's jumped ahead and made the bet Republicans will retain control of Congress and (President) Clinton will win re-election," he said. "But if we're wrong dramatically, the Dow could fall 100 to 150 points" on Wednesday.

Investors were betting that a split in government would prevent Democrats from running deep spending-driven budget deficits and Republicans from cutting taxes and not paying for them with spending cuts.
Signs of Wall Street's confidence also rippled through the bond market.

"The markets think this election is not going to go haywire," said Joshua Feinman, global market economist at Bankers Trust. "They think that at a minimum, the Republicans will hold on to the Senate and that there will be checks and balances, accommodation, and that nothing wild will happen."

The 30-year Treasury bond rose one point, lowering its yield, which moves in the opposite direction from the price, to 6.59 percent -- the lowest since March 26 -- from 6.66 percent at Monday's close.
The bond market's only mild setback was the reaction to the Treasury's $18.5 billion sale of three-year notes.
"The auction of the three-year notes was less than robust," said Michael Moran, chief economist at Daiwa Securities America Inc.
"The market dipped a bit when the auction results came out, but it rebounded later in the day."

The Treasury plans to sell $10 billion of 10-year notes on Wednesday and $10 billion of 30-year bonds on Thursday. The funds are used to repay investors whose bonds are maturing and to fund government operations.
In currency trading, the dollar climbed against major currencies along with stock and bond prices.

The dollar surged to 1.2810 Swiss francs, a 20-month high. It settled at 114.25 Japanese yen and 1.2765 Swiss francs late in New York, up from 113.80 yen and 1.2662 francs late on Monday. It also rose to 1.5200 German marks from 1.5105.

Early election results were expected after polls closed at 6 p.m. EST (2300 GMT) in Kentucky and Indiana, with the polls in seven more states to close at 7 p.m. EST (midnight GMT). Final results from the House and Senate could be delayed by time differences in the West, where there are many critical races.
Elsewhere, December crude oil fell 15 cents to $22.64 a barrel at the New York Mercantile Exchange. December gold settled at $379.60 an ounce, unchanged.
Overseas, London's FTSE index of 100 stocks fell 7 points to 3,921.1 and Tokyo's Nikkei average fell 40.73 points to 20,592.33.
